name: web-research
label: Web research

tools.name: search
tools.use: Search the web and read the top results. Prints a numbered list plus the text of the top 3 pages, so one call usually answers the question.
tools.args: The query as plain words — no quote characters, they become part of it. --read N reads that many pages instead of 3, --read 0 gives links only. --recent day|week|month|year limits by age and is what you want for news. -n N sets list length (default 6). --site DOMAIN restricts to one domain, --region CODE biases to one (uk-en, us-en).
example: best local model for tool calling

tools.name: fetch
tools.use: Read web pages as markdown — headings, lists, tables, code and links kept, navigation and markup discarded.
tools.args: One or more URLs. --max-chars 0 removes the 24,000-character cap, --save DIR also writes each page to a file, --links prints the page's links instead of its text.

tools.name: doc
tools.use: Read a file as text — PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, an image, or anything text. This is how you open a file someone attached: attachments arrive as a path under uploads/ and are the one thing you cannot see without opening.
tools.args: One or more file paths. A scanned PDF or a photo of text is read with OCR automatically — add --lang deu (or fra, spa, ita, por, nld, rus, ukr, swe, nor, dan, fin) when it is not English. --max-chars 0 removes the 24,000-character cap, --save DIR also writes the text out.

tools.name: rg
tools.use: Search inside files you already saved to the workspace.
tools.args: A pattern and a path, relative to the workspace. -n prints line numbers, -i ignores case.

tools.name: jq
tools.use: Filter or reshape JSON, usually from curl or an API response.
tools.args: A jq filter, then a file — or nothing after it to read stdin.

tools.name: curl
tools.use: Call an API or fetch raw HTTP, when you want the bytes rather than a rendered page.
tools.args: -sSL and a URL for a plain GET; -i includes response headers, -X METHOD, -H 'Header: v' and -d BODY shape a request. Use fetch for anything you intend to read as text.

tools.name: wget
tools.use: Download a file or mirror a small path to the workspace.
tools.args: A URL. -O FILE names the output, -q silences progress, -r -np -l N mirrors a small subtree.

tools.name: openssl
tools.use: Inspect a site's TLS certificate — issuer, subject, the names it covers and when it expires — and do the everyday crypto odd jobs: hashes, base64, random bytes.
tools.args: s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName reads a live certificate. Local forms take no network: dgst -sha256 FILE, base64 -d, rand -hex 16.

tools.name: python3
tools.use: Run Python, for anything the other commands cannot express — a custom request, or glue between them.
tools.args: -c and a program, or a script path. requests, lxml, beautifulsoup4, trafilatura, python-docx, openpyxl, python-pptx and Pillow are installed.

notes: Reach for `search` first: it prints the numbered results and the text of the top three pages, so answer from that page text rather than the snippets — and one search is usually enough; if it did not answer, `fetch` one of the URLs it gave you rather than searching again with different words. There is no browser and no JavaScript engine, so a page that renders client-side comes back empty and says so. Use `doc` on a file the user attached — those arrive as a path under uploads/, and for a PDF, a spreadsheet or a scan the path is all you are given. Save pages worth keeping with `fetch --save sources`, then `rg` them, rather than holding whole pages in context. Paths are the same ones the file tools use: write `notes/sources.md`, not an absolute path. Output too large to return inline is kept under /run/ghost-runs/ — reach it with a shell command, not the file tools.
